reason: The picture shows fusion proteins on adjacent muscle precursors, and the chapter says those cells join into fibres.
expectation: The precursor cells will join into a muscle fibre with multiple nuclei.

effect: The precursors fused into one fibre with many nuclei and sliding filaments; its grip sites are still covered.
reaction: It was interesting that one long muscle cell can have many nuclei.
reason: The calcium pulse spreads around the fibre's filaments, so it looks like the next step toward making it pull.
expectation: The calcium signal will let the filaments interact and make the fibre pull.

effect: Calcium uncovered grip sites, letting the filaments slide and the fibre shorten. It still needs to become ready again.
reaction: It was surprising that the filaments slide without shortening themselves.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes have pumps and ATP, suggesting they can return calcium to storage so the fibre can reset.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage, allowing the fibre to relax and become ready again.

effect: Calcium was pumped back into storage, stopping the pull and leaving the fibre ready again. Now both muscles need to be built and attached.
reaction: I didn't expect relaxation to require ATP too.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces, so the relaxed muscle fibre looks like a suitable piece to put into them.
expectation: The fibre will fill the biceps sheaths to help form a muscle with tendons.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs fibres, but either muscle seems like a reasonable place to start.

effect: The fibre needed collagen-rich matrix first, forming bundles called fascicles with enough for both muscles.
reaction: I missed the connective-layer step, but the automatic hint made it clear.
reason: The fascicles are bundles of muscle fibres, and the biceps sheaths have empty spaces for them.
expectation: The fascicles will fill the biceps sheaths to form a muscle with tendons.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs bundles, so I could build it first.

effect: The fascicles filled the biceps sheaths, forming a muscle with tendons; the triceps still needs to be built.
reaction: The picture makes the connection from fibres to tendon clearer.
reason: The result said there were enough fascicles for both muscles, and the triceps sheaths also have empty spaces.
expectation: The fascicles will fill the triceps sheaths to form the triceps with tendons.

effect: The fascicles filled the triceps sheaths, so both muscles are built and need attachment to the skeleton.
reaction: The three triceps heads joining one tendon are clearer now.
reason: The biceps tendons lead toward the shoulder and radius, so the movable arm skeleton looks like the place to attach them.
expectation: The biceps will attach across the elbow to the arm skeleton.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs to attach across the elbow, so it could go first.

effect: The biceps is attached and pulls the radius to bend the elbow; the assembly still has an empty extensor slot.
reaction: The two poses make the biceps' pull easier to picture.
reason: The triceps tendon attaches at the elbow on the opposite side, so it fits the remaining extensor slot.
expectation: The triceps will attach to the arm assembly and help straighten the elbow.

effect: The triceps filled the remaining slot, completing the arm and showing how its attachment helps straighten the elbow.
reaction: Seeing how two pulling muscles produce opposite movements made the assembly feel complete.

mostWorthwhile.text: Attaching the two muscles was most worthwhile: their different positions explain bending and straightening at the elbow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Filling the two sets of sheaths felt a little repetitive, although it showed that both muscles contain bundles.

surprise.text: I was surprised that the filaments slide without shortening and that resetting after a pull uses ATP.

arbitrary.text: I didn't initially see why the fibre needed collagen-rich matrix before going into the sheaths. The automatic hint and resulting picture explained the connective layers.

continue.text: Yes, I would choose another chapter to see how other body parts work together. Connecting the muscles' attachments to opposite movements was interesting.
